Corpus › Conversions & formatting › ↦

↦

Translation status: English reader-locale proof. Term names and code fences follow the en pack; supporting prose may still be English.

Converts a value with explicit runtime parsing or coercion semantics.

Aliases: convert, conversio

Syntax: <expression> ↦ <type> [⊥ <recovery>]

Category#

conversion

Related#

  • ∷
  • ⊥

Examples#

radix/corpus/conversio/conversio.fab (canonical · operator-group)#

Converts a value with explicit runtime parsing or coercion semantics.

# =============================================================================
# ↦ — Converts a value with explicit runtime parsing or coercion semantics.
# =============================================================================
#
# What this teaches:
#   • Core conversion — the `↦` operator converts between types with explicit parsing (string→int) and coercion (int→string).
#   • Default with `⊥` — the `⊥` operator supplies a default value when conversion fails at runtime (`⇥` only names error types).
#   • Chaining — `↦` composes left-to-right for roundtrip conversions.
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • Confusing `∷` (compile-time type ascription) with `↦` (runtime conversion) and using `vel` instead of `⊥` for conversion recovery.
#
# See also: ∷, ⊥
# =============================================================================

# conversion — type conversion operator (↦)
#
# <expr> ↦ <type>
# <expr> ↦ <type><params>
#
# GRAMMAR:
#   convertExpr :← expr '↦' type
#
# EXPECTED OUTPUT:
#   conversio.expected
#
# BACKEND:
#   Siblings radix.fab and bivalens.fab compile-only until Go semantics align.

main {
    # ↦ converts string → int
    let _ n1 ← "42" ↦ int
    # ⊥ supplies a default on failure
    let _ n2 ← "invalid" ↦ int ⊥ 0
    let _ n3 ← "255" ↦ i32
    let _ f1 ← "3.14159" ↦ float
    let _ f2 ← "invalid" ↦ float ⊥ 0.0
    let _ s1 ← 42 ↦ string
    let _ s2 ← 3.14 ↦ string
    let _ s3 ← true ↦ string

    # chained ↦ left-to-right
    let _ roundtrip ← ("42" ↦ int) ↦ string
    print n1
    print n2
    print n3
    print f1
    print f2
    print s1
    print s2
    print s3
    print roundtrip
}

Expected output:

42
0
255
3.14159
0.0
42
3.14
true
42

radix/corpus/bounded/conversio-lista-to-textus-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

Rejected route: a list of strings does not convert to a string.

# =============================================================================
# list to string — rejected route
# =============================================================================
#
# What this teaches:
#   • No list converts to text, whatever its element type; the checker refuses
#     `list<T> ↦ string` with one named diagnostic (need 03277dd2).
#   • Say the meaning instead: list<b8|b16|b32> first, then ↦ string; or the
#     format string "§"(xs).
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • reading ↦ as "join the elements" — it is not a join.
# =============================================================================

main {
    let list<string> a ← ["x", "y"]
    let string s ← a ↦ string
    print s
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/conversio/float-to-int-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

Rejected route: a bare float or decimal to integer conversion has no rounding choice.

# =============================================================================
# float to integer — rejected without a rounding choice
# =============================================================================
#
# What this teaches:
#   • A bare `float ↦ int` is a compile error: the checker refuses it with one
#     named diagnostic (SEM016 float_to_integer_requires_rounding, need ea7cfde1).
#   • Say the rounding: `via Floor`, `via Ceil`, `via HalfEven` or `via Trunc`.
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • expecting `↦` to truncate — there is no default rounding.
# =============================================================================

main {
    let float a ← 2.5
    let int n ← a ↦ int
    print n
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/conversio/textus-to-lista-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

Rejected route: a string does not convert to a list.

# =============================================================================
# string to list — rejected route
# =============================================================================
#
# What this teaches:
#   • A string is not a list of strings — the element type does not say which
#     encoding, so the checker refuses "abc" ↦ list<string> with one named
#     diagnostic (SEM016 textus_to_lista_unsupported, need 5dccc092).
#   • Say the encoding: ↦ list<b8> gives the UTF-8 octets (list<b16> and
#     list<b32> are the wider rows), or build the character list explicitly.
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • reading ↦ as "split the characters" — the element type is not an
#     encoding choice.
# =============================================================================

main {
    let list<string> cs ← "abc" ↦ list<string>
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/conversio/via-bits-retired-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

Rejected route: via Bits is retired; a bit pattern is an explicit ↦ bN.

# =============================================================================
# via Bits — retired spelling for a bit-pattern route
# =============================================================================
#
# What this teaches:
#   • `via Bits` is retired and refused by name (SEM016
#     conversio_via_bits_retired). A bit pattern is an explicit `↦ bN` step,
#     never a hint on the conversion.
#   • Say the width: `let f16 h ← n ↦ b16 ↦ f16` reads the bits, then
#     reinterprets them as the target type.
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • copying the old `↦ f16 via Bits` spelling — drop the `via` clause and
#     step through an explicit bit width instead.
# =============================================================================

main {
    let u16 n ← 15360
    let f16 h ← n ↦ f16 via Bits
    print h
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.
